prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Some feel rain. Some feel the beetle startle in its ghost-part when the bark slips. Some feel musk. Asleep against each other in the whiskey dark, scarcely there. When it falls apart, some feel the moondark air drop its motes to the patch-thick slopes of snow. Tiny blinkings of ice from the oak, a boot-beat that comes and goes, the line of prayer you can follow from the dusking wind to the snowy owl it carries. Some feel sunlight well up in blood-vessels below the skin and wish there had been less to lose. Knowing how it could have been, pale maples drowsing like a second sleep above our temperaments. Do I imagine there is any place so safe it can’t be snapped? Some feel the rivers shift, blue veins through soil, as if the smokestacks were a long dream of exhalation. The lynx lets its paws skim the ground in snow and showers. The wildflowers scatter in warm tints until the second they are plucked. You can wait to scrape the ankle-burrs, you can wait until Mercury the early star underdraws the night and its blackest districts. And wonder. Why others feel through coal-thick night that deeply colored garnet star. Why sparring and pins are all you have. Why the earth cannot make its way towards you.

Leaning together in slumber through the whiskey-colored dark, hardly present at all. As things come undone, certain ones sense the moonless air release its particles onto the uneven, snow-laden hillsides. At why others, through the coal-dense night, sense that richly hued garnet star. At why bickering and needles are the whole of what you possess. At why the world cannot find its path toward you.

# Sensory Landscapes and the Ache of Disconnection

The text builds its emotional and imagistic power through the repeated invocation of "some feel," a phrase that functions almost like a refrain to catalog an astonishing breadth of sensory experience. Through this repetition, the poem gestures toward the vast diversity of human and bodily perception—ranging from the tactile immediacy of rain and the earthy richness of musk to the more intimate and startling image of sunlight rising in the blood vessels beneath the skin. This accumulation of sensations grounds the poem in the physical world while simultaneously suggesting that feeling itself is multiple, layered, and impossible to fully contain.

Complementing these sensory catalogs, the poem draws heavily on natural imagery to establish its setting. Animals such as the beetle, the snowy owl, and the lynx populate the landscape, lending it a vivid, living presence. These creatures are set against a distinctly wintry backdrop of snow, oak, and dusking wind—a world caught between light and darkness, movement and stillness. This carefully rendered environment does more than provide scenery; it creates an atmosphere of cold beauty and quiet vulnerability that resonates with the poem's deeper concerns.

At the heart of the text lies a searching question about safety and survival. The speaker wonders whether any place can truly be secure from destruction, asking pointedly if there is anywhere "so safe it can't be snapped." This question introduces a note of fragility and threat, suggesting that even the most protected spaces remain susceptible to sudden rupture. The imagery of snapping conveys both abruptness and finality, as though safety itself is a delicate thing that can break without warning.

From this anxiety emerges a broader meditation on loss and regret. The speaker's wish that "there had been less to lose" reveals a painful awareness that attachment and abundance carry within them the seeds of grief. To have much is to risk much, and the reflection on "how it could have been" opens a space for mourning not only what has been lost but also the alternative futures that never came to pass. These lines carry the weight of hindsight, of measuring the present against imagined possibilities.

The poem closes on a note of yearning and profound confusion about disconnection. In its final lines, the speaker wonders why the earth "cannot make its way towards you," expressing a longing for a reunion or connection that remains stubbornly out of reach. This closing image captures the ache of separation—the sense that even the world itself, vast and encompassing as it is, cannot bridge the distance between the speaker and the object of their longing. The result is a haunting conclusion that leaves the reader suspended in the same uncertainty and desire that animates the poem as a whole.
outputs.L4:
# On the Threshold of Feeling

There is a way the world arrives at us in pieces. Rain does not fall as a single thing but as a thousand separate touches against the skin, each one a small announcement of being alive. Snow settles differently—slower, quieter—laying its whiteness over the ground until the familiar becomes strange, until the shapes we knew are softened into something we must learn again. To perceive is to be assembled and unmade in the same instant.

Consider the animals moving at the edges of our vision: the deer that pauses and then is gone, the bird whose shadow crosses the window and vanishes. They live so entirely inside their own awareness, without the burden of asking what it means. And above them, indifferent and constant, the moon and the far stars keep their distances. We look up and feel both held and abandoned by that light, which has traveled so long to reach us and asks nothing in return.

This is the fragility the passage insists upon—that to feel deeply is also to be easily broken. The same nerve that registers the warmth of sun registers the cold. There is no way to open oneself to wonder without opening oneself to wounding. We are porous creatures, and the world pours through us.

So we search for safety, for some shelter where the sharpness cannot reach. But safety and disconnection are close cousins. To be entirely protected is often to be entirely alone, sealed off from the very touch we crave. This is the central ache: we long to belong to the world, to be at home among the rain and snow and living things, yet something holds us apart. The world glitters just beyond the glass, unreachable.

And this is where the questions begin—the ones that have no easy answers. Why does the world hold itself at such a distance, when we reach toward it with everything we have? Why must there be *sparring and pins*, the small cruelties and persistent hurts that puncture whatever peace we manage to gather? Why does suffering continue, threaded through even our most tender moments?

The passage does not resolve these questions. It leaves them open, hanging in the air like breath on a cold morning—visible for an instant, then gone. Perhaps that is its truest gift: not an answer, but the permission to keep asking, to stand at the threshold of feeling and awareness and let the whole fragile, aching, luminous world move through us.
outputs.L5:
**Some Nights Are Different**

Some people find sleep the moment their head touches the pillow. Others lie awake for hours, watching shadows shift across the ceiling, waiting for rest that stubbornly refuses to come.

When the house finally grows quiet, and the last light in the neighborhood flickers off, a special kind of stillness settles in. It is in these silent hours that some thoughts, buried during the busy day, rise gently to the surface. We remember old friends, unfinished conversations, and dreams we once held close.

There is something peaceful about the world when everyone else is asleep. The rushing and the noise fade away, leaving only the soft sound of your own breathing. Some find this loneliness heavy, while others treasure it as a rare moment of freedom.

When morning comes, and the first birds begin to sing, those who stayed awake feel the weight of the sleepless night. Yet even they must eventually surrender. Sooner or later, everyone falls asleep, carried away into a quiet, dreaming darkness.

Some memories only visit when we are half-asleep, drifting between waking and dreaming. Perhaps that is why some people say the truest thoughts arrive not during the day, but when the whole world has gone to rest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the style of Franz Wright, using fragmented sensory images and repetition of "Some feel..." Include nature imagery like snow, owls, a lynx, and stars.
counterfactuals.output:
# Some Feel

Some feel the snow before it comes, a pressure behind the eyes, the way the light goes gray and inward, the way silence gathers like a held breath in the throat of the world.

Some feel the owl's passage more than see it—that soft catastrophe of wings unstitching the dark, the small death carried off, the branch still trembling with the memory of weight.

Some feel the lynx watching from the tree line, those eyes like two cold stars fallen and made animal, made patient, made hunger walking on four soundless feet across the frozen field.

Some feel the stars as wounds, as old light still arriving from what has already gone out, and isn't that the way of everything we love, the shining that outlasts the burning source.

Snow now. Snow on the shoulders of the pines, snow filling the tracks the lynx has left, snow erasing, snow forgiving, snow that falls the way sleep falls on the exhausted, the way grace falls, indiscriminate, on the just and the unjust and the merely tired.

Some feel God as this: the owl, the lynx, the star, the snow. The hunter and the hunted and the white indifferent mercy falling over both.

And some feel nothing. And some feel everything. And some lie down in the deepening cold and finally, finally, cannot tell the difference between the falling and the fallen, between the light and what the light has left behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental, dreamlike piece of poetic prose that meditates on distance, loss, and what different beings perceive. Use imagery of animals, weather, and celestial bodies.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Distances Keep

There is a fox who counts the miles between herself and the moon in heartbeats, and finds the number is the same as the distance between a mother and the child she set down like a stone in fast water.

*

Somewhere it is always raining on the place you cannot return to.

The whales know this. They sing across an ocean of static, calling out coordinates for a warmth that has already drifted, continents grinding slow beneath them, the map redrawing itself in the dark. What they perceive is not water but the *shape of absence pressing back*—a wall of nothing you can lean your whole weight against.

*

I have been trying to tell you something about the light from dead stars.

How it arrives anyway. How the sky is a museum of the already-gone, and we look up and call it *beautiful*, we call it *wishing*, we do not say: *this is a letter from someone who no longer exists, still traveling, still insisting.*

*

The owl sees the mouse as heat.
The mouse sees the owl as the last thing.
The field between them sees nothing, being only a field,
being only the green indifferent distance that both of them must cross.

*

And you—

you were weather to me. A front moving in from a country I'd never named. I felt the pressure drop. I felt the animals in me go quiet the way they do before the storm arrives, and then the storm did not arrive, only its promise, only the long held breath of a sky that keeps its rain for someone else, some other field, some farther fox still counting.

*

What does the comet remember of the sun it circles once a lifetime?

Only this: that it is always leaving, always returning, and the two are the same motion. That to love a burning thing is to spend your existence *falling toward and away* in a single unbroken arc, and to call this—

*

—call this *orbit.*
Call this *the only word we have for a wound that has learned to keep its shape.*

*

Tonight the fox lies down in the snow.
Above her the dead stars keep sending their impossible mail.
The whales go on translating the ocean's grief into a music no one surfaces to hear.

And the distance, which perceives nothing,
holds all of it—

holds you, holds me, holds the last warm thing
each animal was reaching for

when the light went out
and kept on
traveling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, surreal paragraph about consciousness and perception in the natural world—include a beetle, a snowy owl, wildflowers, and Mercury as a star.
counterfactuals.output: In the hush before dawn, a beetle carries the whole weight of its knowing across a continent of moss, each footfall a small theorem proving the world exists. Somewhere above, a snowy owl unspools her silence into the dark, and in the mirror of her eye the wildflowers open backward—petals remembering the shape of light before it was ever born. Consciousness, that shy migrant, moves between them like pollen: it does not belong to the beetle or the owl or the trembling blue of forget-me-nots, but drifts, borrowing eyes, borrowing feathers, borrowing the small blind hunger of roots. And low on the horizon Mercury burns—a star, the flowers insist, though the astronomers would frown—flickering its ancient rumor that everything perceiving is also perceived, that the meadow dreams us as surely as we kneel to name it, and that even the dew, holding a single bent reflection of the sky, is a mind briefly, gloriously awake before it falls.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a haunting prose poem that blends the interior and exterior worlds. Weave together images of rain, snow, garnet stars, and the question of whether any place is truly safe.
counterfactuals.output:
# Weather of the Interior

The rain has been falling since before I had a name for it, and still it falls—outside against the glass, inside against the chambers I mistake for shelter. There is no roof that does not eventually remember it was once sky.

I have been asking the question wrong. Not *where* is it safe, but *when*, and the answer arrives always in past tense, always just leaving through the far door as I enter.

Snow now. The rain has learned another language, softer, the vocabulary of forgetting. It settles on the branches of the nerves, on the rooftops of every house I've fled or burned. How gently the cold erases. How it tucks the whole world into a white that could be mercy or could be the beginning of not-being-anything-at-all.

Above the snow, above the rain that fathered it, the garnet stars are burning their slow red patience. They are the color of the heart's deepest room, that muscle no lock protects. I look up and they look through me—those old wounds hung in the dark, still bleeding light after the body that bled them has been ten thousand years extinguished.

*Is anywhere safe?*

The stars do not answer because the stars *are* the answer: even they, those furnaces, those red survivors, are only briefly here. Even they are weather. Even they are passing through.

And so I make my peace with the rain against the window that is also my sternum, with the snow that falls in the field that is also my waiting, with the garnet distance that says *no, nowhere, and this is not the tragedy you feared.*

To be unsafe is to be alive inside the storm of being.

The window weeps. I let it. Somewhere the snow is still arriving, still whitening the dark—and I hold my small warmth like a struck match against the falling, the falling, the endless tender falling of the world into itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the tradition of contemporary American prose poetry—melancholy, associative, and rich with imagery of winter landscapes, blood vessels, smokestacks, and a longing for connection.
counterfactuals.output:
**Vascular Winter**

The city breathes in gray exhalations, smokestacks writing their slow cursive against a sky the color of old bruising. I have been thinking about how the body is mostly rivers—how the blood keeps moving even when we've stopped believing in destinations.

Snow falls the way forgetting falls, particle by particle, until the field is a blank page nobody will write on. My grandmother's hands were maps of blue tributaries, and I used to trace them, thinking: this is how a person carries her whole life close to the surface, this is how the interior insists on being seen.

There is a loneliness specific to industrial towns in January. The way the plumes rise and disperse. The way heat becomes weather. Somewhere a furnace is converting coal into the possibility of morning, and I am standing at a window that reflects only my own wanting back at me.

We are all just trying to reach the extremities. The cold teaches this—how the heart pulls warmth inward, abandons the fingers, the toes, the small far outposts of the self. Triage of the living. I press my palm to the glass and think of everyone I've let go frostbitten, everyone I've called back too late.

The vessels branch like the bare trees branch, like the smoke branches, like the roads leaving town branch toward other towns where other windows hold other faces lit blue by the same reluctant dusk.

I want to tell you something true: that connection is just circulation on a larger scale. That we are all capillaries feeding some enormous body we'll never see the shape of. That the snow keeps falling on the smokestacks and the smokestacks keep breathing and somewhere the blood keeps its ancient tidal appointment, keeps insisting, against all evidence, that it has somewhere warm to go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
